title: Quantitative Aspects of Chemical Change
seo_title: Grade 11 Physical Sciences: Quantitative Aspects of Chemical Change Worksheets (CAPS)
standard_code: Grade 11 Physical Sciences: Quantitative aspects of chemical change
standard_text: Molar volume of gases (22.4 dm³·mol⁻¹ at STP); concentration of solutions; volume relationships in gaseous reactions; limiting reagents; percentage yield; percentage purity; empirical and molecular formulae; titration calculations. (summary of CAPS Physical Sciences, Grade 11, Chemistry: Quantitative aspects of chemical change)
meta_desc: Free Grade 11 Physical Sciences worksheets (CAPS): molar volume, concentration, limiting reagents, percentage yield, percentage purity and titrations. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: At STP one mole of gas occupies 22.4 dm³.
key_sub: The limiting reagent is used up first.
body_html:
How to think about it

Use the mole ratio from the balanced equation to work out amounts of reactants and products. At STP (0 °C, 101,3 kPa) one mole of any gas occupies 22,4 dm³. For gases at the same temperature and pressure, the volume ratio equals the mole ratio.

The limiting reagent is the reactant that is used up first; it decides how much product forms. Percentage yield = actual yield ÷ theoretical yield × 100. In a titration, c₁V₁/c₂V₂ = n₁/n₂ from the balanced equation.

Example

Volume of 2 mol of CO₂ at STP?

n × 22,4

Answer: 44,8 dm³

Example

Theoretical yield 10 g, actual 8 g. Percentage yield?

actual/theoretical × 100

Answer: 80%

Common mistakes

  • Using the reactant in excess to find the product.
  • Using 22,4 dm³ at room temperature.
  • Forgetting the mole ratio in titrations.

faq.q: Why is the actual yield usually less than the theoretical yield?
faq.a: Some product is lost when it is separated, the reaction may not go to completion, or side reactions happen.
The mass of the pure substance divided by the mass of the impure sample, × 100.
